feedback: If a learner orders the higher fossil as the earlier animal — e.g. reasoning 'it's been up there longest' — replay the build-up: each new layer lands ON TOP of the previous one, so the bottom layer formed first. Being higher means it arrived later, not earlier; oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
If a learner says all the layers and fossils formed together, emphasise that layers accumulate one atop another over long stretches of time, so different layers record different times.
Confirm correct reasoning by connecting a fossil's position to WHEN its organism lived: a lower fossil was buried longer ago, therefore that organism lived earlier.
Prompt for landscape change: a sea-creature fossil high on land shows that place was once underwater — so landscapes are not fixed but change over long time.
activities.intendedInsight: The trilobite resting at the BOTTOM must be older than the ammonite above it, because its layer was deposited — and the organism buried — first. Undisturbed rock layers are a stack of time with the oldest underneath, so a landscape's history can be read from its layers.
learnerActions: Deposit sediment one layer at a time as 'time' passes, so each new layer settles on top of the last.
In each era, place/bury an organism in the layer being formed at that time (e.g. a trilobite early, an ammonite later).
Relate the build-up to a jar: pour in sand, then mud, then gravel, letting each settle before adding the next — the first poured ends up at the bottom, mirroring how the oldest layer sits lowest.
Cut into the resulting cliff/cross-section and read it back: order the buried fossils from earliest-lived to latest-lived.
State, in your own words, why the fossil in the lower layer must be older than the one above it.
Reconstruct how the landscape changed over time from the sequence of layers and the fossils in them.
activities.title: Build-up-the-layers time machine

feedback: If the learner cannot connect a fossil's position to when its organism lived, point back to the build-up model: lower layer = buried earlier = organism lived earlier.
Reinforce landscape-change reasoning: ask what a sea fossil high on a hill tells you about that place long ago.
Keep answers to relative order (which came before which); if the learner reaches for exact ages, redirect — you cannot read an exact age off a layer just by looking at it.
activities.intendedInsight: The ordering rule applies to genuine evidence: real rock formations whose layers have not been overturned record a sequence of events, and you can construct the landscape's history from the pattern of layers and fossils rather than memorising a told story.
learnerActions: Examine a real, dramatic strata cross-section (a canyon wall or cliff face) with many visible layers that are flat-lying and not folded or overturned.
Identify which layers are older and younger using the oldest-at-the-bottom rule.
Match named fossils to the layers they appear in and order the organisms by relative time.
Write or say a short explanation of how this landscape changed over a long time, citing the layer/fossil pattern as evidence.
Transfer the reasoning to a second, unfamiliar cliff with undisturbed layers to check you can apply the rule to new evidence.
activities.title: Read real strata and reconstruct the story
